items.prompt:
A book about ocean life has this table of contents:
Chapter 1: Fish and Sharks (page 4)
Chapter 2: Whales and Dolphins (page 18)
Chapter 3: Coral Reefs (page 30)
Chapter 4: Deep Sea Creatures (page 44)
Chapter 5: Ocean Conservation (page 56)

A student needs to write a report about why coral reefs are disappearing and what people are doing to save them. Which chapters would be most helpful, and why would she use two different chapters?

steps: Chapter 3: Coral Reefs (page 30) would explain what coral reefs are and why they might be disappearing.
Chapter 5: Ocean Conservation (page 56) would cover what people are doing to save them.
The student needs two chapters because her question has two parts: the problem (reefs disappearing) and the solution (conservation efforts).
solution.answer: She would use Chapter 3 (Coral Reefs) to learn why coral reefs are disappearing, and Chapter 5 (Ocean Conservation) to learn what people are doing to save them. She needs both because her report has two parts: the problem and the solution.

items.prompt:
A student finds an article with these headings:
'What Is Climate Change?'
'Causes of Climate Change'
'Effects on Animals'
'What Can We Do?'

He wants to write a paragraph about how melting ice is hurting polar bears. He says he needs to read only the 'Effects on Animals' section.

Do you agree? Is there any reason to look at other sections too? Explain.

steps: 'Effects on Animals' would directly tell about polar bears.
However, 'Causes of Climate Change' explains why the ice is melting in the first place.
Understanding the cause would make his paragraph stronger.
He might also look at 'What Can We Do?' to add a hopeful conclusion.
solution.answer: I partly agree. 'Effects on Animals' is the most useful section for polar bears. But looking at 'Causes of Climate Change' would help him explain why the ice is melting, making his paragraph stronger and more complete.

items.prompt:
A nonfiction article has three captions:
Caption A: 'A humpback whale breaches the water near Alaska.'
Caption B: 'Humpback whales can grow up to 52 feet long and weigh 40 tons.'
Caption C: 'Humpbacks were nearly extinct in the 1960s but have since recovered.'

Which caption is most important to understanding the whale's conservation history? Explain your thinking.

steps: Caption A describes where a whale was photographed.
Caption B gives size facts.
Caption C tells about the whale's history: near extinction and recovery.
For conservation history, Caption C is the most important.
It is the only one that mentions time (1960s), past status (nearly extinct), and change (recovered).
solution.answer: Caption C is most important for understanding conservation history because it tells you when whales were nearly extinct (1960s) and that they have since recovered. The other captions describe appearance and size, not history.

items.prompt:
A book about weather has this note on the first page:
'Words in bold are defined in the Glossary on page 62.'

A student reads this sentence: 'Thunderstorms form when warm, moist air rises quickly into the atmosphere, where condensation occurs.' The words 'atmosphere' and 'condensation' are in bold.

Describe the steps the student should take to fully understand this sentence.

steps: The student reads the sentence and notices two bold words.
She knows bold words are defined in the glossary on page 62.
She turns to page 62 and looks up 'atmosphere' and 'condensation.'
She reads both definitions.
She returns to the sentence and re-reads it using the definitions to understand the full meaning.
solution.answer: The student should turn to the glossary on page 62, look up 'atmosphere' and 'condensation,' read their definitions, and then re-read the sentence to understand it fully using those definitions.

items.prompt:
An article about endangered animals has a photo of a snow leopard. The caption reads: 'Only about 4,000 snow leopards remain in the wild as of 2023.'

A different article on the same topic has a photo of a snow leopard, but no caption.

Explain why the caption makes the first article more useful for a student writing a report.

steps: The caption provides a specific number: 4,000 snow leopards.
It also provides a year: 2023, making it current and citable.
For a report, a student needs specific facts, not just a photo.
The captionless article only shows how the animal looks, not how rare it is.
The caption turns the photo into evidence that supports the topic of the report.
solution.answer: The caption makes the article more useful because it gives a specific, current fact: 4,000 snow leopards remain as of 2023. A student writing a report needs precise data, and the caption provides that. The article without a caption only shows what the animal looks like.

items.prompt:
A student reads a digital article about volcanoes. On the side, there is a navigation menu:
Introduction
Types of Volcanoes
Famous Eruptions
Volcano Safety
Photo Gallery

The student already knows what volcanoes are and wants to see pictures of famous eruptions.

Which menu items would she use, and in what order? Explain.

steps: She already knows what volcanoes are, so she skips 'Introduction.'
She wants pictures of famous eruptions.
She might go to 'Famous Eruptions' to read about them.
Then she would go to 'Photo Gallery' to see the pictures.
Order: Famous Eruptions, then Photo Gallery.
solution.answer: She would go to 'Famous Eruptions' first to read about them, then visit the 'Photo Gallery' to see pictures of those eruptions. She skips the Introduction since she already understands the topic.

items.prompt:
A student is reading a book that has no table of contents, no headings, and no glossary.

List three problems the student might have, one for each missing text feature.

steps: Without a table of contents: the student cannot find what page a topic starts on without reading everything.
Without headings: the student cannot skim to find the right section.
Without a glossary: the student cannot look up unfamiliar words.
solution.answer: Problem 1 (no table of contents): The student cannot find where a topic begins without reading the whole book. Problem 2 (no headings): The student cannot skim to find relevant sections. Problem 3 (no glossary): The student cannot look up the meanings of unfamiliar words.

items.prompt:
A student finds two articles about rainforests. Both have the heading 'Threats to the Rainforest.' Article A has this text under the heading. Article B has this text under the same heading with a caption on a photo that reads: 'Satellite images show that an area of rainforest the size of a football field is lost every second.'

The student says Article B is more informative. Do you agree? Explain using what you know about captions as text features.

steps: Both articles have the same heading and presumably similar body text.
Article B adds a caption with a striking specific fact: an area the size of a football field is lost every second.
Captions add information that the text alone does not include.
The fact in the caption is powerful and specific.
Article B provides more information through the text feature of the caption.
solution.answer: I agree. Article B uses a caption to add a specific, striking fact that the text alone does not include. The caption tells us the exact scale of deforestation, making Article B more informative than one with no caption.

items.prompt:
A book about space has this table of contents:
Chapter 1: The Sun (page 4)
Chapter 2: The Inner Planets (page 14)
Chapter 3: The Outer Planets (page 28)
Chapter 4: Moons and Dwarf Planets (page 42)
Chapter 5: Stars and Galaxies (page 58)
Chapter 6: Space Exploration (page 72)

A student wants to compare Earth and Mars. Which chapter(s) would be helpful and why? On what page(s) would she start?

steps: Earth and Mars are both inner planets.
Chapter 2: The Inner Planets (page 14) covers both.
She would start on page 14.
She might also check Chapter 6 to see if space missions to Mars give comparison data.
solution.answer: She would start with Chapter 2: The Inner Planets (page 14) because both Earth and Mars are inner planets, making that chapter the best place for a comparison. She might also check Chapter 6 for information from Mars exploration missions.

items.prompt:
A student reads an article about healthy eating. The article has a heading: 'Foods That Give You Energy.' Under the heading, there is a photo of fruits and vegetables with a caption: 'Foods rich in vitamins and fiber help your body work well all day.'

The student wants to know what specific vitamins do for the body. The article has a glossary.

Describe the full strategy she should use to find this information, using text features.

steps: The heading 'Foods That Give You Energy' points to the right section.
The caption mentions vitamins.
If the word 'vitamins' is in bold, she should check the glossary for its definition.
The glossary would give more detail about what vitamins do.
Strategy: find the section using the heading, read the text and caption, look up 'vitamins' in the glossary.
solution.answer: She should use the heading to find the section about energy foods, read the text and caption, and then look up 'vitamins' in the glossary to find a definition that explains what vitamins specifically do for the body.

items.prompt:
An article about the water cycle has four headings:
'Evaporation'
'Condensation'
'Precipitation'
'Collection'

All four words are also in bold throughout the article and defined in the glossary.

Why does the author make these four words bold and define them in the glossary? What does this tell you about how important these words are?

steps: These four words are the names of the four stages of the water cycle.
They are the key vocabulary of the whole article.
Making them bold draws the reader's attention to them.
Defining them in the glossary ensures readers understand each stage.
Together, bold text and glossary entries signal that these words are central to understanding the topic.
solution.answer: The author bolds and glossary-defines these words because they are the four essential stages of the water cycle. Without understanding these terms, a reader cannot understand the whole article. Both features together signal that mastering these words is essential.

items.prompt:
A student compares two nonfiction books about penguins. Book A has a table of contents, headings, and captions. Book B has no text features at all.

For a research project, which book would be more useful? Give three reasons.

steps: Reason 1: The table of contents in Book A lets the student find topics quickly.
Reason 2: Headings in Book A help the student skim to find relevant sections.
Reason 3: Captions in Book A add specific facts beyond what the text alone says.
Book B has none of these, so the student must read everything to find information.
solution.answer: Book A is more useful because: (1) the table of contents helps find topics quickly, (2) headings let the student skim to find relevant sections, and (3) captions add specific facts. Book B's lack of features makes research much slower and harder.

items.prompt:
An article has this caption under a photo of a city at night: 'Light pollution from cities can make it impossible to see stars from urban areas.'

A student says this caption is a 'hidden argument.' What does he mean? Do you agree?

steps: The caption gives a fact about light pollution blocking stars.
This fact could be seen as a reason to care about light pollution.
It implies that city lights are harmful to astronomy.
A 'hidden argument' means the caption is stating a problem, not just describing a picture.
The caption is more than a label; it makes a claim about an environmental issue.
solution.answer: I agree. The caption does not just describe the photo. It states that light pollution makes stars impossible to see, which implies there is a problem worth addressing. This is a hidden argument embedded in a text feature.

items.prompt:
A book about migration has these glossary entries:
migration (noun): the seasonal movement of animals from one place to another.
route (noun): the path taken to travel from one place to another.
nesting grounds (noun): the area where animals travel to lay eggs or raise young.

A student reads: 'Each spring, Arctic terns follow the same migration route to their nesting grounds in the Arctic.'

Using all three glossary entries, explain what this sentence means in simple words.

steps: Migration = seasonal movement.
Route = the path taken.
Nesting grounds = where they raise young.
Each spring, Arctic terns travel seasonally along the same path to the Arctic, where they lay eggs and raise young.
solution.answer: The sentence means: Every spring, Arctic terns travel along the same seasonal path to the Arctic, where they go to lay eggs and raise their young.

items.prompt:
You are writing your own nonfiction article about honeybees. Your article will have four sections: 'What Bees Look Like,' 'Where Bees Live,' 'How Bees Make Honey,' and 'Why Bees Are Important.'

Describe the text features you would add to your article (at least three) and explain what each one would help your reader do.

steps: Table of contents: lists the four sections with page numbers so readers can find any section quickly.
Headings: labels each of the four sections so readers know what topic is coming.
Glossary: defines key words like 'hive,' 'pollen,' and 'nectar' so readers understand the vocabulary.
Captions on photos: add facts about bees that support the text.
Bold words: highlight key vocabulary words to signal they are important.
solution.answer: Three text features: (1) Table of contents, so readers can find each section by page number. (2) Headings for each of the four sections, so readers know what each part covers. (3) A glossary with definitions of 'hive,' 'pollen,' and 'nectar,' so readers understand the vocabulary. I might also add captions on photos to provide additional facts.
